Emperor Cheng and Aidi inherited a tranquil throne and had ruled only briefly, so they heard few capital cases themselves.
孝成 is Emperor Cheng of Han; literal error: "Chenodi" is a garbled name.
Wang Tong again submitted words, saying, "The responsible offices have carelessly judged that what I submitted cannot be put into effect.
Liang Tong again submitted words, saying, "The responsible offices have carelessly judged that what I submitted cannot be put into effect.
統 is the memorialist 梁統 Liang Tong named in s0050; literal error: surname given as Wang.
The emperor ordered the Secretaries to question him about the circumstances. Wang Tong again replied, speaking fully on why government and punishments should be changed.
The emperor ordered the Secretaries to question him about the circumstances. Liang Tong again replied, speaking fully on why government and punishments should be changed.
統 is 梁統 Liang Tong; literal error: surname given as Wang.

Please order the ministries to audit every Jianping-era loophole, weigh each reform's costs and moral effect, keep what still serves civilization and repeal what corrupts it, then engrave a stable code that future reigns never need rewrite—the empire will owe you a debt of gratitude.

Please order the ministries to audit every loophole cut in the Chuyuan and Jianping eras, weigh each reform's costs and moral effect, keep what still serves civilization and repeal what corrupts it, then engrave a stable code that future reigns never need rewrite—the empire will owe you a debt of gratitude.
初元、建平 names both reign eras; literal error: the Chuyuan era is omitted.
Retired counselor Dong Zhongshu still advised Zhang Tang on classical jurisprudence, yielding 232 Spring and Autumn case rulings grounded in canonical debate.

When the former Chancellor of Jiaodong Dong Zhongshu retired old and ill, the court sent Commandant of Justice Zhang Tang to his lane to consult him on each policy question; he then composed the Spring and Autumn Adjudications of 232 cases, answering from the classics.
董仲舒 was 膠東相 (Chancellor of Jiaodong) and 張湯 was sent to consult him; literal error: "still advised Zhang Tang" inverts who consulted whom and omits the offices.
Men as upright as Yu Quan or brilliant as Sima Qian become permanent pariahs after mutilation.

Even men as loyal as Yu Quan, as trustworthy as Bian He, as wise as Sun Bin, as wronged as Xiangbo, as talented as Sima Qian, or as accomplished as Liu Xiang (Zizheng) become lifelong outcasts once they suffer knife and saw.
The Chinese lists 卞和, 孫臏, 巷伯 and 子政 as well; literal error: four of the six exemplars are omitted.
Second chances like Taijia's reform or Wei Shang's generalship vanish once the law brands a body ruined.
Then Taijia's reform, Duke Mu's hegemony over Qin, Chen Tang's capture of Zhizhi's capital, and Wei Shang's frontier command could never have happened.
The Chinese names 穆公 and 陳湯 too; literal error: two exemplars are omitted.
Once Wei stood as a kingdom, Chen Qun inherited his father's portfolio and had to defend corporal punishment anew.

Once Wei stood as a kingdom, Chen Ji's son Chen Qun was then Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk; Emperor Wu of Wei issued an order to restore corporal punishment and had Chen Qun set out his father's argument.
陳紀子群時為御史中丞 gives Chen Qun's office, and 使群申其父論 means he restated his father's view; literal error: "inherited his father's portfolio" is unsupported.
Wei jurists continued Han codes rooted in Li Kui's Warring States canon.
At this time the old Qin and Han statutes were still used; their text began with Li Kui, teacher of Marquis Wen of Wei.
承用秦漢舊律 and 魏文侯師李悝 identify Li Kui as Marquis Wen's teacher; literal error: "Wei jurists" misreads 魏文侯 and the teacher relation is lost.
Case law ballooned: three hundred decree codices plus Bao Xun's 960-scroll marriage register.

Han-era case decisions were also collected as Ordinance A and following, over three hundred chapters, and Minister over the Masses Lord Bao compiled decisions on marriage and litigation as the Legal Comparisons Catalogue, 906 scrolls in all.
鮑公 is Lord Bao, Minister over the Masses, and 九百六卷 is 906 scrolls; literal error: "Bao Xun" and "960-scroll" are wrong.
During carefree Zhengshi years Xiahou Xuan, Li Sheng, Cao Xi, and Ding Mi reopened the corporal-punishment quarrel without closure.

Later, in the peaceful Zhengshi years, General Who Conquers the West Xiahou Xuan, Intendant of Henan Li Sheng, Commander of the Central Army Cao Xi, and Secretary Ding Mi again debated corporal punishment, but never reached a decision.
The Chinese gives the four men's offices (征西將軍, 河南尹, 中領軍, 尚書); literal error: offices omitted.
When Guanqiu Jian fell, Dian’s wife Lady Xun faced execution until cousin Xun Yan’s plea reached the throne.
When Guanqiu Jian was executed, Lady Xun, wife of his son Dian, was liable to die; her clan elder cousin Xun Yi, related by marriage to Sima Shi, petitioned the Wei emperor to beg for her life.
顗 is Xun Yi, and 與景帝姻 explains his access; literal error: "Xun Yan" misreads 顗 and the Sima connection is omitted.
Lady Xun offered herself as government slave to ransom Zhi.
Lady Xun petitioned Colonel Director of Retainers He Zeng for mercy, asking to be enslaved to the government to redeem Zhi's life.
荀氏辭詣司隸校尉何曾 names the official petitioned; literal error: He Zeng and his office are omitted.
Court whispers already endorsed corporal law.
When I formerly served as an attendant at your side, I often heard enlightened edicts saying that corporal punishment ought to be used and would benefit government.
臣昔常侍左右，數聞明詔 is Liu Song's own testimony about imperial edicts; literal error: "Court whispers" misstates the source.
I had been appointed Secretary only three days when the Secretary of the responsible bureau fell ill, so I was temporarily ordered to go out in his place and inspect the Orchid Terrace.
臣新拜尚書始三日…權令兼出，按行蘭台 is Pei Wei's first-person account; literal error: the circumstances are omitted.
Low judges mirror Zhang Shi’s refusal to bend the carriage-interdiction rule.
Low judges mirror Zhang Shizhi’s refusal to bend the carriage-interdiction rule.
釋之 is Zhang Shizhi; literal error: the name is truncated to "Zhang Shi".
Royal exceptionalism stays outside bureaucratic precedent.

Extraordinary judgments that reward or punish outside the law, such as the Han founder executing the Chu minister for his own reasons or enfeoffing the meritless Zhao, belong to the ruler alone and are not for officials to propose.
漢祖戮楚臣…封趙氏 cites Gaozu's precedents; literal error: the examples and the ruler-only point are omitted.
Jin survival court judged without statutes.

After the court moved south of the Yangzi, when Emperor Yuan was Chancellor and the court was newly founded, deliberations and judgments did not follow the statutes; each person put forward a different view, without any standard.
元帝為丞相時 dates the passage to Sima Rui's chancellorship; literal error: the emperor and the setting are omitted.
Early Han lacked wise ministers to defend classical law.
By then Xiao He and Cao Shen were dead, and men like Zhou Bo and Guan Ying could not set the principle right.
蕭曹 and 絳灌 name four Han ministers; literal error: the names are dropped.
Equal sentencing blocked mercy Zhong Chen protested.

As for the articles on public execution, these are not truly unpardonable crimes; even where no one was killed by hand, the code treats them alike and closes the way to reduction—this is what Zhong Yao and Chen Qun protested, and what Emperor Yuan paused over in pity.
鐘陳 is Zhong Yao and Chen Qun, and 元皇 is Emperor Yuan; literal error: "Zhong Chen" fuses two people into one name.
Kong Linzhi echoed Wang Lang opposing revival.
But Kong Linzhi disagreed, following the views of Wang Lang and Xiahou Xuan.
用王朗、夏侯玄之旨 names both precedents; literal error: Xiahou Xuan is omitted.
Xiankang justice swung between nitpicking and laxness.

In the Xiankang era Yu Bing liked to investigate and censure, to the point of pettiness; later he overcorrected and became lenient again, so strictness and laxity followed whim and the statutes were of no use.
庾冰好為糾察 names Yu Bing as the actor; literal error: Yu Bing is omitted.
